intro: Alfred Cortot recorded the two G♭ major études, Op. 10 No. 5 and Op. 25 No. 9, on this complete 1920 Victor disc side, playing the running triplets of Black Keys and then the clipped leaps of Butterfly. The pause between the two pieces is kept as it was in the original pairing.

sections.label: A · Black Keys, triplets and chords
sections.mNote: The right hand plays on the black keys.

sections.label: B · Black Keys, D♭ major middle section
sections.mNote: Left-hand calls accompany the continuing right-hand triplets.

sections.label: A′ · Black Keys, G♭ major return and close
sections.mNote: The opening returns before wide arpeggios and closing octaves.

sections.label: C · Butterfly, staccato leaps and slurred pairs
sections.mNote: Short right-hand groups mix detached notes with slurred pairs.

cues.title: Black notes, two hands
cues.text: Black Keys begins with right-hand triplets above detached left-hand chords. Chopin writes quick changes from loud to soft: the opening phrase is loud and is answered lower down the piano. The running notes are marked legato.
cues.evidence: Opening articulation and dynamic contrasts: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Étude_Op._10,_No._5_(Chopin). The Alfred Cortot Archives confirms both études on matrix B-23953, take 2, recorded 22 April 1920 at Camden: https://www.cortotarchives.org/recordings/11.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Julian Fontana, 1839
cues.text: On 25 April 1839 Chopin wrote to Julian Fontana from Marseille to ask whether Clara Wieck had played this étude well. He called it “the least interesting” of the études for anyone who did not know it was meant for the black keys, and wished she had chosen something better.
cues.evidence: Chopin to Julian Fontana, Marseilles, 25 April 1839, letter 109 in Chopin’s Letters, coll. Henryk Opienski, trans. E. L. Voynich (New York: Knopf, 1931), p. 199: “the least interesting of the études, — at least for those who do not know that it is on the black keys”. https://archive.org/details/chopinsletters00chop

cues.title: Cortot’s working edition, 1915
cues.text: Cortot also edited the étude and taught it on paper. In his 1915 working edition he gave the aim as “legato brillant, nommé jeu perlé”, brilliant legato, called pearly playing. His exercises prepare the hand to shift between widely separated positions.
cues.evidence: Alfred Cortot, ed., Frédéric Chopin: 12 Études, Op. 10, Édition de travail (Paris: Maurice Senart, 1915, plate E.M.S. 5004), p. 33, Étude V: “Legato brillant, nommé ‘jeu perlé’”, with exercises for the supple shifting of the hand in the “position disjointe” (IMSLP #367492).

cues.title: Second étude, Op. 25 No. 9
cues.text: The second étude is Butterfly, Op. 25 No. 9, also in G♭ major. Its right-hand groups mix short slurs with detached notes and octaves, after the continuous triplets of the first étude.
cues.evidence: The Victor label identifies the pairing; the recording’s established second-piece boundary is retained. Op. 25 No. 9’s articulation: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Étude_Op._25,_No._9_(Chopin).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dedications of Op. 10 and Op. 25
cues.text: Chopin dedicated all of Op. 10, published in 1833, to his friend Franz Liszt. The second set, Op. 25, which includes this Butterfly, appeared in 1837 with a dedication to Marie d’Agoult, Liszt’s companion.
cues.evidence: IMSLP work pages: Op. 10, first published 1833, dedicated to Franz Liszt (https://imslp.org/wiki/Études,_Op.10_(Chopin,_Frédéric)); Op. 25, first published 1837 (Paris: Maurice Schlesinger), dedicated to Comtesse d’Agoult, 1805–1876 (https://imslp.org/wiki/Études,_Op.25_(Chopin,_Frédéric)). Liszt’s relationship with Marie d’Agoult from 1834: https://www.liszt.org/p/chronology.html

transitions.title: D♭ major under the running triplets
transitions.from: A · Black Keys, triplets and chords
transitions.to: B · Black Keys, D♭ major middle section
transitions.how: The first étude modulates to D♭ major. The right hand continues its triplets on the black keys while the left hand changes the bass and the chords. Later in this middle section, short left-hand figures sound beneath the right hand’s sempre legatissimo.
transitions.evidence: Op. 10 No. 5, middle section and marking at bar 33: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Étude_Op._10,_No._5_(Chopin), citing Leichtentritt, vol. 2, pp. 106–108.

transitions.title: Return to G♭ major and the coda
transitions.from: B · Black Keys, D♭ major middle section
transitions.to: A′ · Black Keys, G♭ major return and close
transitions.how: From bar 49 the left hand leads back to G♭ major, and the first étude’s opening figure returns. The dynamic falls to pianissimo. The coda follows with broad arpeggios and ends with a run of black-key octaves in both hands.
transitions.evidence: Op. 10 No. 5, return from bar 49 and coda: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Étude_Op._10,_No._5_(Chopin), citing Leichtentritt, vol. 2, pp. 108–109.

transitions.title: Between two G♭ major études
transitions.from: A′ · Black Keys, G♭ major return and close
transitions.to: C · Butterfly, staccato leaps and slurred pairs
transitions.how: Black Keys ends in G♭ major and the piano stops. Butterfly begins in the same key, marked Allegro assai. The triplets are replaced by short right-hand groups, some slurred and some detached, over a light accompaniment.
transitions.evidence: Victor 64989 label: https://archive.org/details/78_etude-in-g-flat-major-black-keys-etude-in-g-flat-major-the-butterfly_alfred-co_gbia0291196a. Second étude’s key, tempo and articulation: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Étude_Op._25,_No._9_(Chopin).

composer.born: 1 March 1810, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: Composer for the piano, known for music that drew on operatic singing and on the irregular accents of the mazurka.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832 Chopin, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist, played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. He had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers, and teaching soon supplied his living. For the rest of his life his profession depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from one concert city to the next; Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. The family moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
